content: Ankle fractures in children typically result from twisting injuries and vary in complexity and severity. These injuries occur at an annual incidence of 1 in 1000 children. Minor fractures are generally treated with splints or casts, while more severe fractures require surgical fixation using screws, plates, or pins, followed by immobilization. The objective of this study was to evaluate the benefits and harms of various interventions for treating ankle fractures in children. A systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Bone, Joint and Muscle Trauma Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL, up to September 2015. Randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials assessing treatments for ankle fractures in children were included. Two reviewers independently screened studies, assessed bias, and collected data. No meta-analysis was performed. Three randomized controlled trials involving 189 children with clinically diagnosed low-risk ankle fractures were included. These fractures were predominantly classified as undisplaced Salter-Harris type I fractures of the distal fibula. All three trials compared non-surgical management options. The trials were at high risk of bias, primarily due to the inability to blind participants and clinicians to the interventions. Two trials compared the Aircast Air-Stirrup ankle brace with a rigid cast. In one trial (Trial A), the rigid cast was a removable fiberglass posterior splint, while in the other trial (Trial B), it was a below-knee fiberglass walking cast. In Trial A, both the brace and splint were removed after approximately two weeks. In Trial B, the brace could be removed after five days, while the walking cast was removed after three weeks. Low-quality evidence suggested that children treated with ankle braces had better functional outcomes at four weeks compared to those treated with rigid casts. Functional outcomes were measured using the Activities Scale for Kids-performance (ASKp) in Trial A and a modified version of the ASKp in Trial B. In Trial A, the median ASKp scores were 91.9 in the brace group versus 84.2 in the splint group. In Trial B, the modified ASKp scores were 91.3% in the brace group versus 85.3% in the cast group, with a mean difference of 6.00% favoring the brace (95% CI 1.38% to 10.62%). Trial B indicated that a 5% difference in the modified ASKp score was clinically significant. Neither trial reported on long-term outcomes or unacceptable anatomical results. Adverse events were reported with very low-quality evidence. In Trial A, pressure-related complications were twice as common in the brace group (10 of 20 children) compared to the splint group (5 of 20 children). Conversely, Trial B found that unscheduled healthcare visits were four times more frequent in the cast group (16 of 50 children) compared to the brace group (4 of 54 children). Some adverse events in the brace group were linked to the failure to wear a protective sock. There was very low-quality evidence suggesting that children in the brace groups returned to pre-injury activities earlier than those in the cast groups. Trial B also provided low-quality evidence that children preferred wearing an ankle brace for five days or more over being immobilized in a walking cast for three weeks. Moderate-quality evidence indicated no significant difference in pain levels between the two groups at four weeks. The third trial compared a Tubigrip bandage with crutches and advice to a plaster of Paris walking cast for two weeks. This trial included 45 children with inversion injuries of the ankle and reported results at four weeks. Very low-quality evidence suggested little difference in pain and function between the two groups, as measured by a non-validated pain and function score. However, children treated with Tubigrip returned to normal activities approximately six days earlier than those treated with a cast (mean 14.17 days for Tubigrip versus 20.19 days for cast; mean difference -6.02 days, 95% CI -8.92 to -3.12 days). Recent magnetic resonance imaging studies suggest that most injuries in these trials were sprains or bone bruises rather than true fractures of the distal fibular growth plate. In conclusion, low-quality evidence indicates that children with clinically diagnosed low-risk ankle fractures recover self-reported function more quickly when treated with an ankle brace compared to a rigid cast, particularly a non-removable walking cast. However, there is insufficient evidence from randomized controlled trials to guide clinical practice for treating ankle fractures in children. Further research is needed to address key questions regarding the management of these common injuries.
